summary: This experimental document defines a Metadata Extension Block for the DTN Bundle Protocol. It carries extra information that nodes can use to decide how to handle a bundle, such as whether to store or where to forward it.

plainLanguage.summary: A parcel can carry a sticky note with extra hints, like store this or send via that route, so each stop can decide wisely.

questions: how do dtn nodes use metadata
subtitle: Extra information blocks that help DTN nodes make routing and storage decisions.

tldr.problem: Delay-tolerant networks need a way to carry additional metadata about bundles so that nodes can make intelligent decisions about storage and forwarding.
tldr.mechanism: This extension defines a metadata block that fits into the DTN Bundle Protocol, with a flexible format that can carry different metadata types, starting with URIs.
tldr.outcome: DTN nodes can now embed hints with bundles, enabling content-based routing and intelligent storage decisions across a delay-tolerant network.

today: RFC 6258 is an Experimental RFC and remains part of the DTN standardization effort. It defines the metadata extension block mechanism for DTN bundles and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Metadata Extension Block is an extension to the Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN) Bundle Protocol defined in RFC 5050. It adds the ability to carry metadata alongside the bundle payload, allowing DTN nodes to make smarter decisions about how to handle bundles as they move through a network.

Unlike the bundle payload, which is typically processed opaquely (without looking inside), metadata is meant to be visible and usable by DTN nodes. Examples include keywords found in a payload, geographic coordinates, message IDs, or artist and track information if the payload is media. Nodes use this metadata to decide whether to store a bundle locally (for example, in response to a content search) or which neighbor nodes to forward the bundle to.

The metadata block is defined flexibly so that different types of metadata can be carried. One standard type, URI metadata, is defined in this RFC. Other metadata types can be defined and registered separately.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of metadata as a label on a package that tells handlers what is inside without them opening it. Handlers can read the label to decide where the package should go next.

sections.title: Metadata Block Structure
sections.content:
The metadata block follows the standard Canonical Bundle Block Format used by all DTN Bundle Protocol blocks. It contains the following fields:

Block Type Code is 0x08 (assigned specifically for metadata blocks). Block Processing Control Flags (encoded as a variable-length integer) tell nodes what to do if they cannot parse the metadata. Block Data Length specifies the size of the metadata content.

The block includes a Metadata Type field that indicates which format the metadata uses (such as type 0x01 for URI). The Metadata Field then contains the actual metadata formatted according to that type. Optionally, the block can include EID-reference fields that reference endpoint identifiers from the bundle's primary block, though URI metadata blocks must not include these references.

For URI metadata (type 0x01), the metadata field is an array of bytes containing one or more null-terminated URIs. Nodes can define custom URI schemes to encode processing instructions in the metadata itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The block is like a labeled envelope. The label says what kind of hints are inside, the envelope holds the hints, and the hints are formatted so any node can understand them.

sections.title: Processing and Use Cases
sections.content:
When a bundle is created, a node MAY insert one or more metadata blocks based on local policy and the metadata type being used. As a bundle is forwarded through the network, nodes MAY add new metadata blocks or delete existing ones, again following local policy.

When a bundle arrives at a node, any metadata blocks present are made available for use in storage or forwarding decisions. If the receiving node is the bundle's final destination, it can pass the metadata to the receiving application.

A practical use case is content-based storage and retrieval: nodes maintain a cache of bundles indexed by their metadata. When an application requests bundles related to a specific subject or geographic area, the node searches the metadata of stored bundles and retrieves those matching the criteria, even if the full payload has not been examined.

Another use case is intelligent forwarding: metadata about the payload (such as urgency or target region) helps nodes decide which neighbors are best suited to receive the bundle next, rather than flooding it everywhere.
sections.plainLanguage: As a package travels from place to place, handlers can read the label and decide whether to keep it for a customer, or pass it along. They might add new notes too.

sections.title: Security and Encryption
sections.content:
The DTN Bundle Security Protocol (RFC 6257) defines how to protect blocks with encryption and authentication. Metadata blocks interact with security in several ways.

When a ciphersuite uses strict canonicalization (such as BAB-HMAC for hop-by-hop authentication), the metadata block is included in the security calculation, so it is protected from the sending node to the next node along the path.

When a ciphersuite uses mutable canonicalization (such as end-to-end authentication), the metadata block is deliberately excluded from the calculation. This allows intermediate nodes to modify or add metadata as a bundle transits the network without breaking end-to-end authentication, as long as they do not touch the payload.

If an application needs end-to-end confidentiality and authentication for metadata independent of the payload, an extension security block can encrypt the metadata block separately. A bundle can contain multiple metadata blocks, and each can be encrypted separately, allowing some nodes to search and route based on metadata they can decrypt while the payload remains secret.
sections.plainLanguage: Metadata can be protected like a sealed envelope, or it can be left readable so handlers along the way can add notes. Metadata can also be locked separately from the payload.

sections.title: Metadata Types and Registration
sections.content:
This RFC defines only one standard metadata type: URI (0x01). Other metadata types can be registered with IANA to ensure global uniqueness. Metadata type codes 0-191 require a specification, while codes 192-255 are reserved for private and experimental use without requiring registration.

When a node receives metadata of a type it does not support, the block processing control flags determine the outcome: the node can discard just the metadata block and forward the bundle, or delete the entire bundle if it cannot process the block, depending on local policy.

This extensibility allows the metadata block mechanism to support future uses beyond URIs, such as structured metadata formats, cryptographic signatures, or application-specific data.
sections.plainLanguage: The metadata system is designed to grow. Right now, only simple URI labels are standard, but nodes can be designed to handle new kinds of labels as they are invented and registered.

fields.name: Flags (SDNV)
fields.desc: Block processing control flags and EID-reference indicator.

fields.name: EID Ref Count (SDNV)
fields.desc: Number of EID references, if present; 0 for URI metadata.

fields.name: Block Data Length (SDNV)
fields.desc: Length of metadata type and metadata fields.

fields.name: Metadata Type (SDNV)
fields.desc: Type code (0x01 for URI, 0x00 reserved, 192-255 private).

fields.name: Metadata Field
fields.desc: Metadata formatted per type (URIs for type 0x01).
